title: Good Leaders Help Others to Recognize Harmful Patterns in Their Behavior
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article makes the case that people are largely blind to their own behavioral patterns, even though they can spot them easily in others. It argues that a core job of leadership is to observe recurring reactions and triggers in team members and reflect them back without judgment, helping people close the gap between who they are and who they want to be. The piece acknowledges that these conversations can create defensiveness, but insists that leaders who push through the discomfort build a culture where candid pattern-discussion becomes normal and valuable. It closes with a Twain-inspired quip about the necessity of confronting patterns that hold people back.
points: People struggle to see their own behavioral patterns even though they easily notice them in others.
Good leaders observe recurring triggers and reactions in team members and reflect them back nonjudgmentally.
Naming a pattern as an observation, without evaluation, is often enough to spark real self-awareness.
These conversations can create discomfort and defensiveness, but leaders who persist normalize candid feedback.
Leaders who make hidden patterns explicit help people change behavior that would otherwise go unaddressed.
quotes: Patterns are hard to discern when they involve us. We can see patterns in others much easier than the consistent reactions and responses we employ.
The best leaders observe and collect our patterns and then debrief us to the possibility they are getting in our way.
Holding up a mirror for others and discussing patterns isn’t easy.
Leaders first make observations without evaluation (“When a colleague challenges you, your first reaction is to get quiet and withdraw from the conversation.”) and then stand ready to discuss them.
No one gets better without understanding the patterns that get in their way.
To paraphrase Mark Twain, harmful patterns and diapers must be changed for the same reason.
